t:
The rates of basic compensation of officers and members to whom the amendment made by section 101 of this title applies shall be adjusted in accordance with this section, and on and after the effective date of this title, section 102 of the Act approved September 2, 1964 (D.C. Code, sec. 4–823c), shall not apply to any such officer or member whose rate of basic compensation is so adjusted in accordance with this section. Such rates of basic compensation shall be adjusted as follows:

    (1) 
Except as otherwise provided in paragraph (2), (3), or (4), each officer and member receiving basic compensation immediately prior to the effective date of this title at one of the scheduled service or longevity rates of a class or subclass in the salary schedule in section 101 of the District of Columbia Police and Firemen’s Salary Act of 1958 shall receive a rate of basic compensation at the corresponding rate in effect on and after the effective date of this title.
 
    (2) 
Each private in service step 6, longevity step 7, or longevity step 8 in any subclass in class 1, upon completing a minimum of nineteen years of continuous service as a private, including service in the Armed Forces of the United States but excluding any period of time determined not to have been satisfactory service, shall be advanced to longevity step 9 in class 1, and receive the appropriate scheduled rate of basic compensation for such step in the subclass in which he is serving.
 
    (3) 
Each officer in longevity step 7 in class 5 or 8, upon completing a minimum of fourteen years of continuous service in his respective class, including service in the Armed Forces of the United States but excluding any period of time determined not to have been satisfactory service, shall be advanced to longevity step 8 in his respective class, and receive the appropriate scheduled rate or basic compensation for such step in the class in which he was serving.
 
    (4) Each officer or member of the Metropolitan Police force who is performing the duty of a dog handler on or after the effective date of this title shall receive in addition to his basic compensation an additional $580 per annum, except that if a police private is classed as technician 11 in subclass (c) of salary class (1) in the salary schedule, in section 101 of the District of Columbia. Police and Firemen’s Salary Act of 1958 solely on account of his duties as a dog handler, such police private shall not be entitled to the additional compensation authorized by this paragraph.

fable.w: This section mechanically adjusts basic compensation rates and longevity steps for District of Columbia police and fire officers and members, plus a pay supplement for dog handlers. The only tempting hook is the reference to service "determined not to have been satisfactory", but that is an internal personnel determination, not a process that brings outside parties into a federal decision. There is no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside entities, rulemaking authority, or right to sue.
fable.s: Such rates of basic compensation shall be adjusted as follows:

qwen_block.w: This section establishes a formula for adjusting the compensation of federal officers and D.C. police/fire members. It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation with people outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities) before making these adjustments. The process is purely administrative and statutory, involving only government employees and their pay scales.
qwen_block.s: The rates of basic compensation of officers and members to whom the amendment made by section 101 of this title applies shall be adjusted in accordance with this section
qwen_block.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the section adjusts compensation for specific groups (like dog handlers or those with certain years of service), it involves a decision-making process that could theoretically include input. However, the text is purely prescriptive regarding salary calculations and does not mention any consultation, hearing, comment period, or advisory body involving non-federal parties. The actors involved are federal officers and members of the D.C. police/fire forces (who are government employees), and the decision is made by statute, not through a participatory process with outsiders.

opus.w: This section only sets the rules for adjusting basic pay and longevity steps for D.C. police and fire officers and members, plus an extra allowance for dog handlers. It sets up no process that involves people outside the government: no comment period, hearing, rulemaking authority, advisory body, consultation, or right to sue. The phrase about service 'determined not to have been satisfactory' refers to an internal personnel judgment, not outside participation in a decision.
opus.b:
**Step 1.** One phrase might look like a decision process: "excluding any period of time determined not to have been satisfactory service." But nothing here brings in anyone outside the government. The section just sets pay rates and step advancements for D.C. police officers and firefighters. There is no comment period, hearing, rulemaking authority, advisory body, outside consultation, or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines the formula for adjusting the compensation of federal or DC police/fire officers. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or input from parties outside the federal government (such as states, tribes, or the general public) in making a decision. The process is purely internal administrative calculation of employee benefits.
qwen_chat.s: The rates of basic compensation of officers and members to whom the amendment made by section 101 of this title applies shall be adjusted in accordance with this section
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the section involves "participation" because it details specific procedures for officers and members to receive compensation adjustments based on their service history. However, this is merely an administrative calculation of benefits for federal employees (or DC police/firefighters acting under federal statute), not a process where outside parties consult with the government on a decision. The actors involved are the government and its employees. There is no consultation with states, tribes, the public, or private entities.
